original_question: Does there exist an ergodic automorphism whose absolutely continuous spectrum has finite multiplicity?
target_in_paper: Section 1, Q4: the weakened Banach problem asking for the existence of an ergodic automorphism with finite-multiplicity absolutely continuous spectrum.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the core existential problem in Section 1, Q4: it asks about an ergodic automorphism and about finite multiplicity on the absolutely continuous side of the spectrum. It is also narrower than the broader neighboring Question Q3 and weaker than the simple Lebesgue-spectrum problem Q2, which is exactly how Q4 is positioned in the paper.
missing_details: It should specify that the automorphism is measure-preserving and acts on a probability space; the surrounding discussion is in the setting of measure-preserving automorphisms of probability spaces.
It should identify which spectrum is meant: the spectrum of the associated Koopman unitary operator, conventionally on the subspace orthogonal to the constants.
It should make explicit that the absolutely continuous part is intended to be nonzero; otherwise the question becomes vacuous if one allows transformations with purely singular or discrete spectrum.
It should clarify that 'finite multiplicity' refers to the spectral multiplicity on the absolutely continuous part of the Koopman spectrum, not to total spectral multiplicity in some unrelated sense.
It should state the reference measure for absolute continuity: Lebesgue measure on the unit circle in the spectral representation.
To stay paper-faithful, it helps to note that this is presented as a weakened form of Banach's problem, immediately after Q2.
refined_question: Does there exist an ergodic measure-preserving automorphism T of a probability space (X, B, mu) such that the Koopman operator U_T on L^2(X, mu) orthogonal to the constants has a nonzero absolutely continuous spectral part with finite spectral multiplicity (with absolute continuity understood with respect to Lebesgue measure on the unit circle)?
justification: The draft is closest to Q4 in Section 1, not to Q2 or Q3. Q2 asks for an automorphism with simple Lebesgue spectrum, which is stronger than your draft. Q3 is broader, asking generally which spectra and multiplicity sets can occur. Q4 isolates exactly the finite-multiplicity absolutely continuous question and the author explicitly says this can be viewed as a weakened Banach problem. The nearby context in Q2 supplies the probability-space/orthogonal-to-constants spectral setting, and Theorem 1.1 shows why Q4 is the intended target by linking it to mixing automorphisms of positive local rank: if such a transformation failed higher-order mixing, one would obtain a solution to this weakened Banach problem. The abstract also flags positive local rank as a condition ensuring finite spectral multiplicity, which matches the surrounding intent.
